section_summary: This section continues a reference report on Japanese nationalist and national socialist parties, tracing their leaders, platforms, factional disputes, elections, wartime activity, and dissolution. An appendix then lists important labor unions and begins profiles of their political alignments, officers, reorganizations, and suppression. The section ends during the profile of a clandestine communist labor federation.

subfiles.title: Great Japan Youth Party
subfiles.about: History of the party's officers, nationalist platform, internal disputes, and replacement by the Great Japan Sincerity Society.
subfiles.summary: The entry resumes with Hashimoto Kingorō's followers and the party's leadership, ideology, and 1937 program. It recounts expulsions, financial controversy, anti British and pro China war activity, and the October 1940 dissolution and reconstitution of the group.

subfiles.title: Great Japan Production Party
subfiles.about: Eleven years of the Great Japan Production Party's organization, political activity, and successor society.
subfiles.summary: Founded in Osaka in 1931 by Uchida Ryōhei and Amur River Society associates, the party promoted nationalist political and economic reforms and became involved in labor disputes, elections, and violent right wing politics. The entry follows its internal splits and its reactions to the February 26 Incident, China war, European war, and proposed wartime political changes. In 1942 it reorganized as the Great Japan Renovation Society, retaining many officers.

subfiles.title: Great Japan Sincerity Society
subfiles.about: The successor to Hashimoto's Great Japan Youth Party and its wartime influence.
subfiles.summary: The society was founded in November 1940 as a nominally cultural organization. Its officers continued political activity through the Imperial Rule Assistance movement and the Great Japan Assistance Manhood Group, before the society weakened.

subfiles.title: Great Japan Party
subfiles.about: The Great Japan Party's platform, officers, wartime demands, and dissolution.
subfiles.summary: Formed by Sasai Itchō's faction in 1940, it advocated Axis cooperation and expansion in East Asia. It dissolved after the 1942 Diet election, and its members formed Yamato Musubi.

subfiles.title: Labor Japan Party
subfiles.about: Formation and decline of the Labor Japan Party.
subfiles.summary: The party formed in 1934 from two national socialist groups and lost influence after secessions, electoral failures, and its president's death.

subfiles.title: Imperial Way Society
subfiles.about: The society's shift from reservist leadership to agrarian activism and its suppression.
subfiles.summary: Founded in 1933 by army reservists and farmers, the society later came under Hirano Rikizō's agrarian faction. Financial trouble and political disputes weakened it; police closed several branches in 1942.

subfiles.title: People's Association
subfiles.about: Organization and merger of the People's Association.
subfiles.summary: Akatsu Katsumarō and Tsukui Tatsuo founded it in 1933. After unsuccessful 1936 Diet campaigns, it dissolved and contributed to the Japan Reform Party.

subfiles.title: Enlightened Way Society
subfiles.about: The society's leadership, campaigns, internal divisions, and dissolution.
subfiles.summary: Founded in 1933 after Ishihara Kōichirō broke with Ōkawa Shūmei's circle, the society advocated nationalist unity, political reform, and assertive foreign policy. Its standing suffered from the February 26 Incident and Ishihara's withdrawal, but it resumed campaigns concerning China and European powers. After Tanaka Kunishige's death, members chose to establish a successor alliance.

subfiles.title: Japan Reform Party
subfiles.about: Electoral origins and dissolution of the Japan Reform Party.
subfiles.summary: Several right wing groups joined after the 1937 election. Disagreement over Konoe's planned party led to Etō's departure and the party's dissolution in 1940.

subfiles.title: Japan National Socialist Party
subfiles.about: The party's foundation, split between socialists and nationalists, and renaming.
subfiles.summary: Akatsu Katsumarō founded the party in 1932 from labor and agrarian groups. Ideological disputes drove out major factions; the remaining organization became the Patriotic Political League in 1934.

subfiles.title: 3-6 Club and Fresh Rice Plant Club
subfiles.about: A nationalist discussion club, its activities, and its renamed successor.
subfiles.summary: The club promoted imperial ideology and participated in the campaign against Professor Minobe. Suspicions following the February 26 Incident prompted police scrutiny; it changed its name in 1938 and later faded.

subfiles.title: New Japan Construction League
subfiles.about: Matsutani Yōjirō's nationalist labor organization and its merger.
subfiles.summary: The league formed in 1932, called for a controlled economy and nationalist labor unions, and merged into the Labor Japan Party in 1934.

subfiles.title: New Japan People's League
subfiles.about: The league's foundation, factional secessions, and successor party.
subfiles.summary: Shimonaka Yasaburō organized the league in 1932 to unite national socialists. Leadership disputes and arrests diminished it; Sasai Itchō helped form the Japan Reform Party in 1937.

subfiles.title: Eastern Society
subfiles.about: The Eastern Society's electoral rise, wartime opposition, repression, and decline.
subfiles.summary: The entry traces the society from a discussion group into a nationalist party with Diet members and an agrarian appeal. Under Nakano Seigō it campaigned for aggressive policy abroad while repeatedly changing its formal political status. Its opposition to the Tōjō cabinet led to police restrictions and mass arrests in 1943. Nakano's suicide that October ended its political influence.

subfiles.title: Yamato Musubi
subfiles.about: The Great Japan Party's nominal wartime successor.
subfiles.summary: Formed in May 1942 under Sasai Itchō, it advocated mobilization for war but soon became dormant.

subfiles.title: Appendix III: Important Labor Unions
subfiles.about: Contents list of labor unions profiled in the appendix.
subfiles.summary: Lists fourteen Japanese labor unions and federations.

subfiles.title: Patriotic Labor Unions All-Japan Discussion Society
subfiles.about: A nationalist labor federation formed in 1936 and dissolved in 1940.
subfiles.summary: Twelve unions promoted it; it anticipated the wartime production service movement and dissolved in 1940.

subfiles.title: Japan Labor League
subfiles.about: The league's national socialist alignment and factional division.
subfiles.summary: Founded in 1932, the league split in 1933 over support for the Japan National Socialist Party. Its remaining members rejoined other federations in 1934.

subfiles.title: Japan Labor Unions Conference
subfiles.about: The left wing union federation's communist connections and suppression.
subfiles.summary: Founded in 1925, it joined the Profintern and was ordered dissolved after the 1928 arrests.

subfiles.title: Japan Labor Unions Council
subfiles.about: A democratic trade union council active from 1932 to 1940.
subfiles.summary: The council defended trade unionism as affiliates dwindled; political restrictions forced its dissolution in 1940.

subfiles.title: Japan Labor Unions General Conference
subfiles.about: The left wing federation's platform and 1934 merger.
subfiles.summary: Organized in 1931, it withdrew from party politics and merged into a new national conference in 1934.

subfiles.title: Japan Labor Unions General League
subfiles.about: The federation's shift toward nationalist production service.
subfiles.summary: Established in 1926, it moved from the political center toward nationalist alliances, became the Japan Labor Service League in 1938, and dissolved in 1940.

subfiles.title: Japan Labor Unions National Conference
subfiles.about: Formation and police suppression of a left wing labor federation.
subfiles.summary: Formed by a 1934 merger, it was officially dispersed in 1937 alongside the Japan Proletarian Party.

subfiles.title: Japan Labor Unions National Congress
subfiles.about: The clandestine Profintern affiliate's foundation and suppression.
subfiles.summary: Kokuryō Goichirō founded it in 1928; arrests ended reported activity after 1936.
